lesson.title: The Single Lowest Point: Defining the Global Minimum
lesson.summary: A global, or absolute, minimum is the single smallest value a function attains anywhere on its domain, found by the same endpoint-and-turning-point search used for the global maximum.
lesson.body:
A function has a global minimum at x = c if f(c) is less than or equal to f(x) for every x in the domain of f. As with the global maximum, this is a claim about the entire domain at once, f(c) must be beaten by nothing, not merely by the values immediately around it. Together, global maximum and global minimum are often referred to jointly as global extrema, and the phrase applies whenever either one is being discussed generically.

The search strategy mirrors the one used for the global maximum exactly: on a closed interval where a continuous function's global extrema are guaranteed by the Extreme Value Theorem, list the candidates, the two endpoints plus any interior turning points, evaluate the function at each, and pick out the smallest value.

Return to the same function used for the global maximum, f(x) = x^3 - 3x on [-2, 2], since it is continuous on a closed interval and its candidates have already been located: the endpoints x = -2 and x = 2, and the interior turning points x = -1 and x = 1, where f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 equals zero. The four function values were computed already: f(-2) = -2, f(-1) = 2, f(1) = -2, and f(2) = 2.

Comparing -2, 2, -2, and 2, the smallest value is -2, and again it happens twice, once at the endpoint x = -2 and once at the interior point x = 1. So the global minimum value of f on [-2, 2] is -2, attained at both x = -2 and x = 1.

Notice the tidy symmetry: the same four candidate points supplied both the global maximum and the global minimum, just sorted to opposite ends of the value list. This is typical, one pass of evaluating all the candidates usually answers both questions at once. It is also worth flagging what these particular interior candidates, x = -1 and x = 1, turn out to be: they are not just global extrema on this restricted interval, they are also local extrema of the function in a stronger sense that does not depend on the interval boundaries at all. That distinction, between an extremum that depends on where you chose to stop looking and one that does not, is exactly what the next two sections make precise.
